analysis.one_liner: Cuts acid rain pollution from power plants, factories, and vehicles through enforceable emission limits.
analysis.headline: The Acid Deposition Control Act of 1989, which would have forced power plants to cut sulfur dioxide from 2.0 to 1.2 pounds per million Btu by 1998 and tightened vehicle and diesel standards, died in committee without a single cosponsor or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Clean Air Act to fight acid rain. It required every state to cap sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions from power plants and industrial boilers, tightened pollution standards for cars and trucks, and capped the sulfur allowed in diesel fuel. It used a tradeable allowance system so utilities could bank and trade emission permits to cut costs, and directed states to shield ratepayers from disproportionate bill increases.
analysis.who_benefits: People living downwind of coal-fired power plants — especially in the Northeast, where acid rain was damaging lakes, forests, and buildings — would have breathed cleaner air and seen acid deposition fall. The bill's ratepayer protections and innovation grants were designed to keep electricity bills from spiking. Indirectly, producers of low-sulfur coal and pollution-control equipment would have gained new demand.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every state to adopt plans cutting power plant sulfur dioxide emissions to a statewide average of 2.0 pounds per million Btu by 1994 and 1.2 by 1998, with nitrogen oxide capped at 0.6 by 1998 — the pollutants that cause acid rain.
Extends similar sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide limits to industrial boilers and to industrial process sources by 1998, so factories share the cleanup burden rather than only utilities.

Caps sulfur in highway diesel fuel at 0.05 percent by weight after January 1, 1991, and tightens tailpipe standards for nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons on cars and trucks built after model years 1990-1992.

Lets utilities buy, sell, and bank emission allowances so cuts happen where they are cheapest, and requires state plans to prevent unnecessarily disproportionate increases in electric rates in any region or service area.

Authorizes federal grants and a state option to levy a fee of up to 0.25 mills per kilowatt hour to fund innovative pollution-control technologies, with studies weighing employment dislocation from fuel switching.

analysis.who_pays: Coal-burning electric utilities would bear most of the compliance cost, some of which would likely reach their customers through rates despite the bill's protections. High-sulfur coal producers and the miners who dig it would face reduced demand as utilities switched fuels or installed scrubbers. Oil refiners would pay to produce low-sulfur diesel, and automakers would pay to meet tighter tailpipe standards.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal utilities, their ratepayers, high-sulfur coal miners, refiners, automakers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for utilities would likely be passed on to electricity customers, particularly in Midwest states burning high-sulfur coal; the bill acknowledges this by requiring states to prevent disproportionate ratepayer effects, but it does not eliminate the cost.
Pushing utilities away from high-sulfur coal threatened mining jobs; the bill itself directs regulators to weigh 'employment dislocation associated with fuel switching' when funding cleanups.

The bill built in a congressional off-ramp: after a 1994 study of phase I results, Congress could vote to stop the tougher phase II requirements from ever taking effect, weakening the long-term guarantee.

It restricted allowance trading to units within a single state in phase I and within broad regions in phase II, a narrower market than a national trading system, which economists generally expect to raise compliance costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real, measurable gains — less acid rain in damaged lakes and forests, less sulfur and smog pollution from power plants, factories, and vehicles — at a genuine but concentrated cost to utilities, coal regions, and ratepayers. Its design softened the blow with tradeable allowances, banking, ratepayer protections, and innovation funding, though the geographic limits on trading and the congressional option to cancel phase II in 1995 were real weaknesses. On balance, the environmental and public health benefits were broad while the costs were borne by identifiable industries and their customers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to two subcommittees, where it sat without a hearing or vote until that Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Representative David Obey introduced the bill on August 4, 1989; it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On October 6, 1989 it was split between the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment and the Subcommittee on Energy and Power, and no further action was ever taken.
The bill never attracted a single cosponsor and was never brought to a markup or floor vote before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

Acid rain controls did not die with this bill: the following year Congress passed and President George H.W. Bush signed the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990, which created a national sulfur dioxide allowance-trading program modeled in part on the market approach this bill sketched, though with nationwide rather than state-limited trading.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal-burning utilities and high-sulfur coal producers gained roughly two more years without binding emission limits, and they ultimately got the 1990 law's more flexible national trading market instead of this bill's state-restricted system and tougher ratepayer protections. The public still received acid rain cuts, just through a different vehicle and on a slower track.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal utilities and high-sulfur coal producers, briefly

for.name: Rep. David Obey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Acid Deposition Control Act of 1989 to cut the power plant, industrial, and vehicle emissions that cause acid rain.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership (Chair John Dingell)
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or floor vote; it sat in subcommittee for the rest of the Congress. Dingell, whose Michigan district encompassed auto interests and who was widely reported as a skeptic of mandatory acid rain controls burdening Midwest utilities and automakers, controlled the committee calendar.

against.name: Coal-burning utilities and high-sulfur coal interests
against.what_they_did: Widely reported to have lobbied against mandatory acid rain legislation during the late-1980s Clean Air Act debate, citing compliance costs and coal-mining job losses.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had a single Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors, so the record shows no partisan split either way.

industries.note: The bill would have forced statewide cuts in sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide from their plants, with allowances that could not be freely traded across state lines in the first phase. Utilities would likely have recovered much of the cost from customers, which is why the bill required ratepayer protections.

Utilities meeting the emission rate limits would have shifted toward low-sulfur coal or scrubbers, cutting demand for high-sulfur coal and the jobs tied to it; the bill itself required weighing employment dislocation from fuel switching.
A hard cap of 0.05 percent sulfur in highway diesel from January 1, 1991 would have required refinery upgrades, while delivering cleaner air for people near roads.

Tighter nitrogen oxide limits for cars and light trucks from model year 1991, hydrocarbon limits for trucks, and mandatory onboard vapor-recovery or control technology would have raised per-vehicle costs.

industries.industry: Low-sulfur coal producers and pollution-control equipment makers
industries.note: Utilities seeking cheap compliance would have bought more low-sulfur western coal and scrubbers, and the bill created grant funding, backed by a state fee option, for innovative control technologies.
